summary: Reviewed recent commits and worktree summary, current-state documentation, roadmap index and its two open threads, and all 56 existing proposal scopes. Recent changes include the multisport analysis redesign and milestone celebrations; the current uncommitted recovery change aligns with the existing ache follow-up proposal. Inspected analysis-page accessibility labels and focus states, plus the milestone implementation notes. General navigation accessibility and card-linked coaching already have proposals, and the remaining roadmap threads are explicit. No sufficiently distinct new proposal was identified. Source/documentation review only; no application tests or model calls were run, and no credentials, databases or private training records were opened.

ideas.title: One trustworthy check before shipping
ideas.problem: Frontend behavior tests exist without an npm test command. The backend test command depends on a local dependency folder and mixed import roots. Some tests also use dates that age out of the period they query.
ideas.proposal: Create a documented project check command that runs frontend behavior tests, the frontend build, and backend tests in a reproducible environment. Repair confirmed fixture and clock assumptions without weakening behavior assertions.
ideas.benefit: Make every new feature faster to verify and catch regressions before they reach your training workflow.
acceptance_criteria: One documented command runs the relevant frontend and backend checks from a fresh dependency environment.
Tests do not fail merely because today's date changes.
Strength comparison fixtures include the schema the production code needs.
Existing failing assertions are investigated; no tests are deleted or weakened to obtain a passing run.

ideas.title: Pick up where you left off in Data & Sync
ideas.problem: The selected source on Data & Sync is kept only in component state. Opening a link or refreshing returns to Strava even when you were reviewing another source.
ideas.proposal: Keep the active source in a validated URL query parameter. Preserve it across refresh and browser navigation, and make direct links to Apple Health, HealthFit, and Fitbod work.
ideas.benefit: Return directly to the import source you were working on and share precise troubleshooting links.
acceptance_criteria: A direct URL can select any of the four existing source panels.
Refresh and browser Back/Forward restore the selected source.
Unknown source values fall back safely to Strava.
Switching panels never starts an import.

ideas.title: A smoother dashboard without a mouse
ideas.problem: The app shell provides a main landmark, while Data & Sync nests another main inside it. Repeated navigation and unclear landmark structure add friction for keyboard and screen-reader users.
ideas.proposal: Audit the app shell and page wrappers for a single main landmark, add a visible-on-focus skip-to-content link, and check focus placement after route changes. Keep the current visual design.
ideas.benefit: Make the dashboard easier to navigate with a keyboard and clearer for assistive technology.
acceptance_criteria: Each route exposes exactly one main landmark.
The first keyboard shortcut target is a usable skip-to-content link.
Visible focus remains clear on desktop and mobile layouts.
A browser smoke check covers keyboard navigation on Dashboard and Data & Sync.

ideas.title: Keep unfinished set entries when you switch away
ideas.problem: The live strength runner stores reps and weight in component state until Log set succeeds. syncInputs replaces those inputs from saved or target values when the current set changes or the session reloads, so an unfinished entry can disappear after switching exercises or refreshing. Completed-set persistence does not cover this draft state.
ideas.proposal: Keep a small local draft keyed by workout and set ID for unsubmitted reps and weight. Restore it when returning to the same active set, clearly label it as not logged, and offer an explicit discard action. Reconcile drafts with the latest server state before restoring so another tab or a completed workout cannot silently be overwritten. Keep the existing Log set action as the only completion step.
ideas.benefit: Avoid retyping or forgetting the reps and load you just entered when you check another exercise or accidentally refresh mid-workout.
evidence: frontend/src/views/StrengthWorkoutSession.vue: syncInputs and currentSet watcher replace unsaved input values
frontend/src/views/StrengthWorkoutSession.vue: changePosition calls syncInputs after changing the current exercise/set
frontend/src/views/StrengthWorkoutSession.vue: completeCurrentSet persists values only through the explicit completion API
frontend/src/views/StrengthWorkoutSession.vue: onMounted loads saved session state; localStorage usage currently concerns rest sound
docs/sprints/sprint-36-first-party-strength-workout-tracking.md: durable completed sets and live session runner
acceptance_criteria: Editing reps or weight, switching to another set, and returning restores the unfinished values for the original set without changing the other set.
Reloading the same active workout restores the draft with a clear Not logged label; no completion request is sent automatically.
Successful logging or explicit discard clears that set draft; failed logging preserves it for retry.
Completed, abandoned, deleted, or server-updated sets do not silently receive stale draft values; conflicts offer an explicit review or discard choice.
Unavailable browser storage does not prevent logging; explain that draft recovery is unavailable. Tests use synthetic workout data and cover navigation, reload, failed saves, and stale drafts.

ideas.title: Reopen last week’s specialist advice
ideas.problem: AI team reports are saved under a week-specific settings key, but get_analysis always derives the current week. The Completed weeks view renders SundayReview, which reads the separate weekly-review history. Once the calendar advances, the inspected UI has no way to reopen an older saved specialist report and its HEAD COACH synthesis, even though that report remains stored.
ideas.proposal: Extend Completed weeks with a clearly labeled list of saved specialist analyses alongside existing Sunday summaries. Add bounded read-only list and week-detail endpoints and a shareable selected-week URL. Render the original stored report with its generation time and through-date; do not regenerate it or combine it with present-day recovery context. For older reports without saved citation labels, show honest unavailable-evidence states rather than inventing historical context.
ideas.benefit: Revisit the advice and tradeoffs you were given before deciding whether a training change helped, without spending another AI run.
evidence: backend/app/services/team_analysis.py: read_saved_analysis and save_analysis use team_analysis:{week} keys; get_analysis derives only the current week
backend/app/routers/coaching.py: GET /coaching/team-analysis exposes no historical week parameter or listing
docs/specs/001-hybrid-coaching-team/plan.md: per-week AI persistence and separate completed Sunday history
acceptance_criteria: With synthetic saved analyses for two weeks, both appear in a bounded history list and each can be reopened through a selected-week URL.
Opening a historical report uses its saved specialist text, HEAD COACH synthesis, generation timestamp and through-date, with no AI request or plan write.
Sunday summaries remain available and are clearly distinguished from specialist analyses, including weeks with only one report type.
Missing or deleted supporting activities are labeled unavailable; current recovery or profile data is never silently inserted into historical advice.
Invalid weeks, missing reports, empty history and API failures have clear states; tests cover Monday rollover and verify stored reports remain unchanged.

ideas.title: Find exercises for the equipment you have
ideas.problem: The Workout Studio exercise explorer supports muscle selection, name search and supporting-muscle inclusion, but cannot narrow results by available equipment. The new exercise-guide catalog already contains equipment metadata, so users currently need to inspect individual guides to find movements compatible with their gym or home setup.
ideas.proposal: Add an optional equipment filter to the existing exercise explorer, using explicitly mapped equipment requirements from the guide catalog. Keep the unfiltered list as the default and label exercises with unknown requirements separately. Combine equipment selection with the current muscle and name filters. This is a browsing aid: adding an exercise remains explicit and does not replace an existing movement or transfer its load prescription.
ideas.benefit: Build a workout more quickly when you have limited equipment or a preferred station, without opening every exercise guide.
evidence: frontend/src/components/StrengthExerciseExplorer.vue: explorer-filters and matches currently use query and includeSupporting
frontend/src/activity-detail/exercise-library.mjs: filterExercises filters muscle membership and exercise name
frontend/src/activity-detail/exercise-guides.mjs: getExerciseGuide returns explicit equipment metadata for matched aliases
frontend/tests/exercise-guides.test.mjs: conservative alias matching leaves ambiguous exercise variants unmapped
acceptance_criteria: With no equipment filter, the existing results and ordering remain unchanged.
Equipment filtering composes with muscle selection, supporting-muscle inclusion and name search, with an accessible labeled control and accurate result count.
Exercises with multiple known requirements match only when all required items are available; bodyweight and unknown equipment have distinct states.
Unknown or ambiguously mapped exercises are labeled Equipment unknown and are never presented as verified matches; users can explicitly include or inspect them.
Browsing or changing filters never modifies a saved workout. Adding a movement uses the existing explicit draft action without assuming equivalent loads or automatically substituting exercises.
Synthetic filter tests cover combined requirements, unknown metadata, conservative aliases and reset behavior; keyboard and narrow-screen checks cover the controls and empty state.

ideas.title: Check coaching advice before changing its prompt
ideas.problem: The weekly coaching helper is changing from separate specialist calls to one consolidated call. The inspected helper tests use canned model responses and prompt-string assertions, while backend tests check validation, stale snapshots and persistence. These checks do not show whether a prompt revision improves the actual advice or loses important tradeoffs.
ideas.proposal: Create a small developer-only suite of wholly synthetic weekly snapshots and a review rubric. Support an explicit comparison run of a baseline and candidate prompt using the same scenarios and model configuration, with saved outputs displayed side by side. Start with missing evidence, competing sport goals, a single hard ride in an otherwise ordinary week, and incomplete cycling-power coverage. Separate deterministic schema/citation checks from human judgments about evidence use, tradeoffs, uncertainty and the single proposed change. Keep model runs opt-in and outside the ordinary offline test command.
ideas.benefit: Make coaching prompt changes faster to assess and catch plausible-sounding regressions before trying them on a real training week.
evidence: scripts/team_coaching_helper.py: team_prompt and run_review now produce all specialist reports and HEAD COACH synthesis in one call
scripts/test_team_coaching_helper.py: test_one_consolidated_call_and_one_save supplies a canned response; prompt tests assert text inclusion
backend/tests/test_team_analysis.py: tests cover persistence, stale input rejection, citations and output length rather than generated advice quality
backend/app/services/power_trends.py: build_cycling_power_coaching_context documents missing-coverage and all-time-record interpretation limits
docs/roadmaps/roadmap-v3.md: engineering track targets service/API contracts; a synthetic prompt comparison workflow would complement those checks
acceptance_criteria: At least four versioned synthetic snapshots cover the named scenarios and include a short expected-behavior rubric without prescribing exact wording or one mandatory training recommendation.
An offline command validates fixtures and stored output structure/citations without reading the application database, calling a model, or contacting the running app.

An explicit model comparison command uses only the selected synthetic fixtures, bounds the number of calls, and records prompt hash, model configuration, scenario ID and run timestamp for both outputs.

The comparison artifact shows baseline and candidate advice side by side, distinguishing mechanical failures from human review judgments; it makes no unsupported claim that a single sample proves quality.
The workflow never saves a coaching review or changes a plan. Ordinary tests cannot trigger paid model runs, and a failed comparison preserves previously saved comparison artifacts.

ideas.title: Ride structured workouts in Zwift straight from the plan
ideas.problem: Recent riding is dominated by unstructured Zwift pacer group rides: the 28-day intensity focus is about 73% low aerobic and 3% anaerobic, with no hard sessions in the latest week. Planned ride days carry only an intent and a duration, so there is no concrete interval prescription to execute or judge afterwards.
ideas.proposal: Add a deterministic library of structured cycling workouts (recovery, endurance, tempo, sweet spot, threshold, VO2 max) defined as FTP-relative steps. Let a planned ride day reference a library workout, show its steps with watt targets from the stored FTP, and export it as a Zwift .zwo file. Expose the library through MCP so the planner can assign workouts.
ideas.benefit: Turn intended quality sessions into rides you can start in Zwift in one step, with targets that scale to your Zwift FTP.
evidence: backend/app/models/plans.py: WeeklyPlanDay has intent and duration but no workout structure
acceptance_criteria: Each library workout has an ID, intent, total duration and FTP-relative steps.
A planned ride day can reference a workout and the Plan view shows its steps and a .zwo download.
Exported .zwo files use FTP fractions so Zwift scales them to its own FTP setting.
Watt targets in the app state which stored FTP and date they use.
The library is readable through MCP; unknown workout IDs are rejected.

ideas.title: Notice when training volume quietly slides
ideas.problem: Weekly minutes fell from 706 to 457 to 342 over three consecutive weeks and fitness drifted down from mid-August, but no surface calls out a multi-week decline unless you read the charts yourself.
ideas.proposal: Detect two or three consecutive weeks of falling volume or fitness that do not match a planned lighter week. Show one compact dashboard alert that asks whether it was planned or life-driven, store the answer, and pass it into weekly coaching context.
ideas.benefit: Catch unplanned detraining early and let coaching distinguish a deliberate deload from a stressful stretch.
acceptance_criteria: The alert triggers on a documented rule over completed weeks only.
Weeks planned as lighter do not trigger it.
The athlete can label the drop as planned, life or illness/injury, and the label reaches coaching context.
No alert is shown when data coverage is insufficient.

ideas.title: Three-tap morning check-in including stress
ideas.problem: Subjective state is only recorded as post-activity feedback, so readiness goes stale (the latest check-in is a week old) and nothing captures life stress or sleep, which currently affect training more than load does.
ideas.proposal: Add a daily check-in, independent of activities, with energy, soreness, stress and sleep quality plus an optional pain/niggle score. Make it reachable in a few taps from mobile. Feed it into readiness so high-stress days bias toward easier sessions.
ideas.benefit: Keep readiness current and let the plan respond to stressful days without requiring a hard test or a completed workout.
acceptance_criteria: One check-in per day can be saved and edited without an activity.
Readiness uses the latest check-in and reports when it is missing or stale.
High stress or poor sleep produces visible, conservative guidance rather than silent plan changes.
The check-in fits a 390px viewport and is completable in three taps plus submit.

ideas.title: Suggest an FTP estimate without a test
ideas.problem: The stored FTP is 242 W from March and drives power-based training load, zones and workout targets. A maximal test is not appealing during a stressful period, and recent best efforts come from submaximal group rides, so a guessed value would be no better.
ideas.proposal: Compute a transparent FTP estimate from recent measured power (e.g. best efforts and sustained steady work) with the rides it came from and an explicit uncertainty note. Flag when the stored FTP is old or clearly inconsistent. Never write the estimate automatically; the athlete decides whether to log it.
ideas.benefit: Keep load and workout targets honest without forcing a maximal test.
acceptance_criteria: The estimate cites the efforts it uses and states that submaximal data can underestimate FTP.
A stale-FTP flag appears when the stored value is older than a documented threshold.
No FTP metric is created without an explicit user action.
Insufficient recent power data yields an unavailable state, not a number.

ideas.title: Recovery days that keep the streak and count as rest
ideas.problem: The daily streak is a deliberate goal and planning notes forbid rest days, while readiness flags seven active days out of seven as a risk. The planner already schedules easy sessions, but load and readiness do not treat a genuine recovery day differently from any other session.
ideas.proposal: Define a recovery day by a documented cap (e.g. a short walk, mobility or Z1 spin under a load threshold). Such days extend the streak, count toward rest in readiness and fatigue reads, and are proposed by the planner when fatigue or stress is elevated.
ideas.benefit: Protect the long streak without letting it block real recovery.
acceptance_criteria: Recovery-day criteria are documented and deterministic.
A qualifying day keeps the streak and is not counted as a training day in readiness.
Planned recovery days show the cap they must stay under.
Exceeding the cap is visible after the fact without breaking the streak.

ideas.title: Use one weekly strength target everywhere
ideas.problem: The active process goal and planning notes target three strength sessions per week, but the strength consistency summary uses a hard-coded target of two, so weeks can look hit on one surface and missed on another.
ideas.proposal: Derive the consistency target from the active strength-frequency goal when one exists, falling back to the current default otherwise.
ideas.benefit: See one consistent answer about whether a strength week counted.
acceptance_criteria: With an active strength-frequency goal, consistency uses its target.
Without one, the previous default is used.
A test covers both cases.

ideas.title: Structured return-to-run progression
ideas.problem: Running rules (reintroduce only while heel symptoms stay stable; never raise pace and distance in the same week) live only in free-text planning notes, and run heart rate averages are high for base rebuilding.
ideas.proposal: Track run-specific heel pain after each run and the next morning, a staged progression, a check that blocks raising pace and distance in one week, and an easy-run heart-rate cap. Park until running becomes a focus again.
ideas.benefit: Rebuild running confidently when the focus shifts back from cycling.
acceptance_criteria: Progression stage and heel scores are visible per run.
A plan that raises both pace and distance in one week is flagged before saving.
Easy runs above the heart-rate cap are marked in execution quality.

ideas.title: Correct the reason you gave for a quieter week
ideas.problem: The new volume alert hides its entire component after a reason is saved. Although the service supports updating the week-specific label, the inspected frontend exposes no control for revisiting that answer. An accidental tap can therefore leave an incorrect reason in coaching context.
ideas.proposal: Keep a compact saved-answer row for the currently evaluated volume-drop week, showing its date range and chosen reason with a Change action. Reuse the existing label endpoint to correct the same week explicitly. Keep the full warning dismissed after a successful save and show an inline retry state if a correction fails. This is a correction path for the existing alert, not another alert system.
ideas.benefit: Let the athlete fix an accidental answer quickly and keep coaching context aligned with what they meant.
evidence: frontend/src/components/VolumeTrendAlert.vue: root v-if requires trend.alert; label emits the response that hides the component
backend/app/services/volume_trend.py: build_volume_trend returns the saved label with alert false for a labeled sliding window
backend/app/services/volume_trend.py: save_volume_trend_label updates the same week on conflict
frontend/src/views/Dashboard.vue: onVolumeTrendLabeled replaces the dashboard trend
backend/tests/test_volume_trend.py: test_label_hides_alert_and_is_reported covers dismissal but not a visible correction path
acceptance_criteria: After saving a reason for a synthetic sliding week, the full alert disappears and a compact row shows the saved reason, evaluated week and a keyboard-accessible Change action.
Changing the reason updates the same week through the existing endpoint; a reload and coaching-context read return the corrected reason.
A failed correction preserves the last confirmed answer and offers retry without showing an unsaved choice as persisted.
Refreshing into a different evaluated week cannot send a pending correction to that new week; the user is asked to reopen the relevant current control.
Synthetic UI checks cover saving, correction, failed saves and reload at desktop and 390px widths. Merely opening the control never writes an answer.

ideas.title: See aerobic fitness improve without a test
ideas.problem: Aerobic progress during a cycling base block is invisible unless you do a maximal test, which you are avoiding for now. Power records only move on hard efforts, so steady endurance rides produce no fitness signal.
ideas.proposal: For steady rides of 45 minutes or more with power and heart rate, compute heart-rate drift (Pw:HR decoupling between the first and second halves) and efficiency (average power per heartbeat at endurance intensity). Show an 8–12 week trend on Cycling power with the qualifying rides listed, and let the coach say things like 'same power, 6 bpm lower than in August'.
ideas.benefit: Lets you watch indoor winter base fitness improve from normal Zone 2 rides, with no test and no extra fatigue.
acceptance_criteria: Only rides that meet documented steadiness, duration and data-completeness rules qualify; others are listed as excluded with a reason.
Each trend point links to its ride and shows decoupling percent and power-per-heartbeat.
Indoor and outdoor rides can be compared separately.
Fewer than three qualifying rides in the window yields an unavailable state, not a trend line.
Coach context receives a compact summary and no FTP is written.

ideas.title: Know when shoes, chain and tyres are worn out
ideas.problem: Worn-out run shoes are a common, silent injury risk, and your heel history makes this matter as running returns. Chains and tyres also wear on a schedule nobody remembers.
ideas.proposal: Add a small kit list (shoes, bike, chain, tyres, trainer) with a start date and replacement threshold. Assign kit to activities automatically by sport, with a manual override, using Strava gear where it exists. Show distance used and a calm 'nearly due' cue on Today and in the return-to-run panel.
ideas.benefit: Replace shoes before they cost you a heel flare-up, and stop guessing how old your chain is.
acceptance_criteria: Kit items can be created, retired and given a distance or time threshold.
New runs and rides are assigned to the default kit for their sport, and the assignment can be changed.
Accumulated distance updates when activities are added, deleted or reassigned.
Items at 90% of threshold show a nearly-due cue; retired items keep their history.

ideas.title: Train toward a target event with a countdown and taper
ideas.problem: Seasons and goals describe months and totals, but nothing models a specific day you want to be fresh for: a gran fondo, a 10K or a spring sportive. The planner cannot taper or build toward a date.
ideas.proposal: Let you set one A-event (and optional B-events) with date, sport and type. Show a countdown with the current phase (base, build, peak, taper, recovery) derived from weeks remaining. Give the planner and coach the phase so the last 7–14 days reduce volume while keeping some intensity, and add a race-week checklist (fuelling plan, kit check, travel).
ideas.benefit: Gives the long streak a destination, and makes sure you arrive at the event fresh rather than tired.
acceptance_criteria: An event can be created, edited and removed; at most one A-event is active.
The phase is computed deterministically from weeks remaining and is visible on Today and Plan.
Planning context includes the phase, and taper weeks show a reduced-volume target.
After the event date, the countdown is replaced by a recovery week prompt and the event is kept in history.

ideas.title: Suggest life-load tags from your calendar
ideas.problem: Life-load tags only work if you remember to add them. Busy days, travel and late events are usually already in your calendar.
ideas.proposal: Read the local macOS calendar for the coming week (read-only, on this machine only) and suggest life-load tags for crowded days, travel and late evenings. Show suggestions next to the plan for one-click accept or ignore; never tag automatically or send event titles to the AI coach.
ideas.benefit: The planner keeps hard sessions off chaotic days without you entering your schedule twice.
acceptance_criteria: Calendar access is opt-in and can be turned off; without access the feature is hidden.
Suggestions show the reason (e.g. '6 h of events', 'travel') but store no event titles.
Only accepted suggestions become life-load tags.
Coaching context receives tags only, never raw calendar data.

ideas.title: Add your own voice to the weekly review
ideas.problem: The HEAD COACH weekly review is built from data. It cannot know what felt good, what was hard emotionally, or what next week looks like, unless you write it into a planning brief separately.
ideas.proposal: Before generating the Sunday review, ask three optional questions: best moment, hardest moment, and anything coming up next week. Save the answers with the week and include them in the review and next week's planning context. Show your own words at the top of the saved review.
ideas.benefit: Reviews and plans reflect how training actually felt, and you build a journal of your season for free.
acceptance_criteria: All three questions are optional; skipping still generates the review.
Answers are saved per week and editable after the review is generated.
Saved reviews display the athlete's answers separately from coach text.
Next week's planning context includes the 'coming up' answer.

ideas.title: A short monthly letter from your coach
ideas.problem: Weekly reviews are detailed but short-sighted. Month-scale wins such as new records, streak milestones, sleep trends and goal progress are spread across pages and easy to miss.
ideas.proposal: On the first days of each month, offer a one-click letter covering the previous month: three wins (records, streak, consistency), one pattern noticed (from what-worked memory, sleep debt or life load) and one focus for next month. Keep a list of past letters.
ideas.benefit: A motivating look back that shows progress the weekly view hides, and one clear focus for the month ahead.
acceptance_criteria: Generation is explicit (one click), never automatic.
Wins cite the underlying records or numbers, with links.
Past letters are listed by month and stay unchanged once saved.
A month with little data produces a short honest letter rather than invented wins.

ideas.title: Put a mountain day into the training plan
ideas.problem: Saved routes and route ideas live on the Mountains page, separate from the weekly plan. A big Tatra day is effectively a hard, long session, but the planner does not know about it. Daylight, the forecast and seasonal trail closures are also not checked against the route.
ideas.proposal: Add 'Plan this hike' on a saved route or route idea. It puts the hike on a chosen day as a planned session with estimated time and ascent, so the planner keeps the day before easy and the day after light (lifts stay, per the anchor goal). Add a pre-trip check: walking time against daylight (sunrise/sunset), the mountain forecast for that day, any seasonal trail closures on the route from a small maintained list, and a short packing and fuelling list scaled to duration.
ideas.benefit: Mountain days stop clashing with hard rides, and you know before you leave whether the route fits the daylight and the weather.
acceptance_criteria: A saved route or route idea can be added to a chosen plan day as a hike session with its time and ascent.
Planning context treats a hike above a documented time or ascent as a hard day and adjusts adjacent days without removing lift sessions.
The pre-trip check flags when estimated walking time plus a margin exceeds daylight for the date.
Routes crossing a trail in the closure list for that date show a warning naming the section.
Without forecast data, the check says so instead of showing a default.

ideas.title: One place to see whether lifting is building muscle
ideas.problem: Lifting three times a week is meant to build muscle, but the signals are spread out: per-exercise progression on each session, the protein tick, and body weight in metrics. Nothing answers 'is this working?' over a month.
ideas.proposal: Add a monthly muscle-gain panel on Strength. Show weekly hard sets per muscle group against a simple target range, the share of lifts that progressed (from strength progression), protein-tick adherence on lift days, and the body-weight trend against a gentle gain rate. End with one deterministic suggestion, for example 'legs got 4 hard sets a week; add a set of split squats'.
ideas.benefit: Lets you see whether the Lift 3× anchor goal is turning into muscle, and which single lever to pull if it is not.
acceptance_criteria: Hard sets are counted per muscle group from logged sets using a documented exercise-to-muscle mapping.
Weight trend uses a smoothed rolling average and shows unavailable when there are fewer than a documented number of weigh-ins.
The suggestion never proposes fewer lift sessions per week.
Each number links to or names the sessions it came from.

ideas.title: Check whether last week's focus actually happened
ideas.problem: Each week now ends with one focus, but nothing looks back to see if it was done. Advice that is never checked slowly loses weight.
ideas.proposal: Store each week's focus in a checkable form where possible (e.g. 'two Zone 2 rides', 'protein on all lift days'). At the end of the next week, evaluate it from data, or ask a one-tap yes/partly/no when it cannot be measured. Show the result as the first line of the next wins card and give the coach a short follow-through history.
ideas.benefit: Closes the loop on coaching advice, and repeated misses become visible patterns the coach can address.
acceptance_criteria: Each saved focus records whether it is data-checkable and how.
The next week's card shows done, partly or missed, with the evidence or the athlete's answer.
Unmeasurable focuses ask once and accept no answer without blocking anything.
Coach context includes the last four focuses and their outcomes.

ideas.title: Turn trail coverage into a season goal
ideas.problem: The Mountains page shows what is left to walk, but coverage and summits are not part of goals, the year view or coach context. Hiking progress does not count toward anything.
ideas.proposal: Allow goals such as 'walk 30% of TPN trails in 2027' or 'reach 10 new summits this season', measured from trail coverage. Show them on Goals with a pace forecast that respects the hiking season, and celebrate new trail and summits in the session win.
ideas.benefit: Gives mountain trips a long-term target and makes each new trail section count.
acceptance_criteria: Coverage-percentage and summit-count goals can be created for a park and a date range.
Progress uses the same coverage numbers as the Mountains page.
Forecasts skip off-season months unless they are explicitly included.
A hike that adds new trail or a new summit shows it in the session win.

ideas.title: Turn planned dinners into a shopping list
ideas.problem: The new dinner planner connects recipes and portions to a week, but shopping still requires opening each recipe and manually combining ingredient quantities. Repeated ingredients and changed portions make that translation tedious.
ideas.proposal: Add an explicit Shopping list action to the dinner planner for selected days. Scale recipe ingredients to planned portions, combine matching product IDs or conservatively normalized unlinked names, and retain links to contributing dinners. Let the athlete exclude items already at home and copy the remaining list. Show free-text dinners and ingredients without usable quantities in a separate needs-review section; never invent quantities or log food as eaten.
ideas.benefit: Makes an existing dinner plan easier to carry out and reduces repeated ingredient arithmetic before shopping.
evidence: frontend/src/components/DinnerPlanner.vue: the weekly board supports recipe selection, portion editing through RecipeDrawer, copying last week and logging as eaten, but has no shopping-list action.
backend/app/services/dinner_plan.py: build_dinner_week exposes recipe IDs and planned servings; dinner_log_items already resolves recipe ingredients for the planned portions.
backend/app/services/recipes.py: _clean_ingredients retains grams, free-text amount and optional product_id; serving_items demonstrates scaling by planned servings divided by recipe servings.
frontend/src/food/recipe.mjs: ingredientRow preserves product identity and quantity fields, supporting conservative grouping without guessing ingredient equivalence.
backend/tests/test_dinner_plan.py: synthetic tests already cover recipe portions and weekly dinner planning, providing fixtures for a derived-list contract.
acceptance_criteria: Users can select dates within the displayed week and preview a list containing only dinners on those dates; an empty selection has a clear empty state.
A synthetic recipe containing 300 g of an ingredient for two servings contributes 150 g when one serving is planned; repeated compatible items sum correctly across selected dinners.
Product-linked items merge only by matching product ID; unlinked items merge only by conservative name normalization, and distinct product IDs or ambiguous units remain separate.

Ingredients without usable gram quantities and dinners without recipes remain visible with their original amount text and source dinner under needs review; no guessed conversion is presented as a measured quantity.
Users can mark items already available and copy the remaining list with quantities and selected dates; clipboard failures leave selectable text available.
Changing selected dinners or portions and refreshing the preview recomputes quantities; generating or copying a list never changes dinner plans, recipes or food logs.

ideas.title: Come back from the mountains without a crash
ideas.problem: Mountain days are well handled: a daily hike, Travel kit lifts and no rides. The days after the trip are not. A week of daily hikes leaves legs and sleep in debt, yet the next week is planned like any other. The first home lift is whatever comes next in the A–D rotation, at loads from before the trip.
ideas.proposal: When a run of 3 or more Mountains days ends, open a short re-entry window, like return from illness. It lasts about half the trip length (2–4 days). The first 1–2 days are easy rides only, with no intervals. The first lower-body lift is held at pre-trip loads with 2+ reps in reserve, and upper-body lifts resume as normal. Lifts are never dropped, per the lift anchor. Show a 'Back from the mountains' hint in the readiness panel. Add the window to the dashboard payload and get_recent_context, so the planner keeps intensity out until it ends.
ideas.benefit: Bank the fitness from a big hiking week instead of losing the next week to heavy legs or an early hard session.
evidence: backend/app/services/life_load.py: mountains tag and mountain-day helpers
backend/app/services/illness_return.py: window and RPE-cap pattern to reuse
acceptance_criteria: A run of 3+ consecutive Mountains days starts a re-entry window the day after the last one; shorter runs do not.
Window length scales with trip length and is capped at 4 days.
Briefs inside the window cap ride effort and hold lower-body loads; no lift session is removed or shortened.
The lift volume top-up adds no leg accessory sets inside the window.
The window appears in the dashboard payload, get_recent_context and the planning prompt.
Backend tests cover trip lengths, a trip ending on a Sunday, and overlap with an illness-return window (the stricter cap wins).

ideas.title: Never lose your training history
ideas.problem: All decisions, food logs, strength sessions, coach notes and stall blocks live in one SQLite file, data/training.db, mounted into the backend container. Nothing backs it up, so a bad migration, an accidental delete or a disk problem would lose data that cannot be re-imported from Strava.
ideas.proposal: Take a consistent daily snapshot with SQLite's online backup API (safe while the app runs) into data/backups/. Keep 7 daily and 4 weekly copies, and run PRAGMA integrity_check on each. Also snapshot before schema migrations run at startup. Show the last backup time and status on Data & Sync. Add just backup and just restore <file> recipes, where restore stops the stack and keeps the replaced file aside.
ideas.benefit: Experiment with new features and migrations knowing that yesterday's data is always one command away.
evidence: justfile: no backup or restore recipe
acceptance_criteria: A backup is created at least once a day while the app runs, and before migrations at startup.
Backups are taken with the SQLite backup API, not a file copy of a live database.
Retention keeps 7 daily and 4 weekly copies and deletes only older backup files.
Each backup passes an integrity check, and a failure is shown on Data & Sync.
just restore puts a chosen backup in place and keeps the replaced database file.
A backend test backs up and restores a temporary database and compares row counts.

ideas.title: Your 2026 season on one page
ideas.problem: The Dashboard has cumulative year charts and the coach writes a monthly letter, but nothing pulls the whole year together. Records, the streak, summits, lifts that progressed and the comeback from illness and the heel are spread across separate pages.
ideas.proposal: Add a Season in review page, offered from 1 December and kept for past years. It shows totals by sport against last year, the longest streak, records set (power curve, lifts, runs), summits and trail coverage gained, lifts that progressed most, the best month, and goals completed. Close with a short coach paragraph that uses the monthly letters as input. Reuse existing services and add no new tracking.
ideas.benefit: See a full year of work in one place, which helps motivation going into the winter block.
acceptance_criteria: The page is reachable for the current year from 1 December and for any past year with data.
Totals by sport compare with the previous year when it has data, and omit the comparison when it does not.
Every number links to, or matches, the page it came from (records, Mountains, Strength).
The coach paragraph is generated on request and saved, not regenerated on every visit.
Empty sections are hidden instead of showing zeros.

ideas.title: See which plates to load for each set
ideas.problem: The workout runner shows a target weight per set, and warm-up sets can be added by hand. For barbell lifts you still work out the plates per side yourself, and warm-ups are guessed set by set.
ideas.proposal: For barbell exercises, show plates per side under the target (for example '20 + 5 + 1.25'). Bar weight and available plates come from a small setting on the Athlete page. When a target cannot be made exactly, show the nearest weight you can load and leave the target unchanged. Add an optional 'Suggest warm-ups' button that adds 2–3 warm-up sets ramping to the first working set, using the existing warm-up set type.
ideas.benefit: Spend rest periods resting instead of doing plate maths, with sensible warm-ups for heavy sets.
acceptance_criteria: Barbell sets show plates per side; dumbbell, machine and bodyweight sets do not.
Bar weight and the plate inventory can be edited and persist.
An unloadable target shows the nearest loadable weight and never changes the stored target or progression.
Suggested warm-ups are ordinary warm-up sets that can be removed, and are never counted as working sets.
A frontend test covers the plate breakdown, including targets below the bar weight.

ideas.title: Legs get trained every week
ideas.problem: The A–D lift rotation runs over three lift days a week, so some weeks plan no lower-body work at all. The volume top-up then patches legs with accessory sets instead of a real leg day. Plan follow-through also shows lower-body lifts are the ones most often replaced by rides (3 of 8 done).
ideas.proposal: When strength templates are assigned to a week, guarantee at least one lower-body-dominant session. If the next rotation slot would leave legs out, swap in the leg template for one day and push the skipped template to next week, so the rotation stays fair over a fortnight. Put the leg day on the most reliable weekday (Mon–Wed, according to follow-through), away from hard rides. Mark the swap on Plan with a small 'legs this week' tag.
ideas.benefit: Every week gets a real leg stimulus, which serves the muscle-gain anchor goal, without adding lift sessions.
evidence: docs/roadmap.md open thread: Legs every week
acceptance_criteria: A generated week with three lift days always contains at least one session whose template trains legs, unless legs are a protected body area
The rotation over any two consecutive weeks still uses every template at least once
The leg session prefers Mon–Wed and is never placed the day before or after a planned hard ride when another slot is available
Plan shows a tag on the day that was swapped in, and a test covers the swap and the deferral

ideas.title: Keep leg lifts and hard rides apart
ideas.problem: Nothing stops the planner or a manual move from putting a lower-body lift the day before a sweet-spot or VO2 ride, or right after one. Both sessions then come out worse. With quality rides coming back into the plan, this clash will happen more often.
ideas.proposal: Add a clash rule to plan generation and plan adjustments: a lower-body lift and a hard ride (sweet spot, threshold, VO2) should not land on consecutive days, or on the same day unless the athlete chose that. The planner tries to swap days first. When the athlete moves a session into a clash, show a one-line warning with a 'swap instead' option rather than blocking the move. Upper-body lifts are exempt.
ideas.benefit: Quality rides and leg sessions both land on fresh legs, so each one does more good.
evidence: docs/roadmap.md open thread: Lift and hard-ride clash rule
acceptance_criteria: Generated plans contain no lower-body lift on the day before or after a hard ride when a non-clashing arrangement exists
Moving a session into a clash shows a warning that names both sessions and offers a swap
Upper-body lift days and easy or Z2 rides never trigger the warning
Unit tests cover the clash detection and the swap

ideas.title: A recap page for each mountain trip
ideas.problem: The October 19–25 trip will be a week of daily hikes. Mountains shows trail coverage and single hikes, but nothing celebrates the trip as a whole. A week like that disappears into the weekly totals.
ideas.proposal: Build a trip recap page for any run of consecutive days tagged mountains. Show big count-up numbers for distance, ascent, hours on foot and new trail kilometres. Add a map of every route from the trip on one canvas, a day-by-day strip with each day's peak or highlight and elevation profile, and the trip's share of the season's ascent. Link the page from Mountains, from the re-entry card, and from the Season in review page.
ideas.benefit: The trip becomes a lasting, motivating memory in the app, in the same style as the season review.
acceptance_criteria: Consecutive mountains-tagged days with hikes form one trip, and each trip has its own recap URL
The recap shows animated totals for distance, ascent and time, plus new trail kilometres when coverage data exists
All the trip's GPS tracks are drawn on one map, and each day has a card with its elevation profile
Mountains lists past trips, and the re-entry card links to the recap

ideas.title: A winter cycling arc instead of week-by-week plans
ideas.problem: Each week is planned on its own. Ride-type balance shows sweet spot and VO2 have both disappeared, and plan follow-through shows quality rides were planned only twice in 12 weeks. With nothing describing where winter is heading, weeks drift toward Z2 by default.
ideas.proposal: Add a winter arc: a few blocks running from November to February (for example base, then sweet-spot build, then a VO2 touch, with a lighter week every 3–4 weeks). The arc sets a target ride-type mix and weekly hours for each block, and the weekly planner reads the current block as a constraint. Show the arc as one horizontal strip on Plan's header or on Goals, with 'you are here'. Keep three lift days and minimum weeks intact. The arc only shapes rides.
ideas.benefit: Quality rides come back on purpose, and the winter has a visible direction.
evidence: docs/roadmap.md open thread: Winter base-to-build arc
acceptance_criteria: The athlete can create, edit and clear an arc made of dated blocks, each with a focus and a target ride mix
The weekly planner context includes the current block, and generated weeks include the block's key ride types
Lighter weeks in the arc lower planned ride hours without removing lift days
The arc strip shows the current block and the weeks left in it

ideas.title: Eat enough before the sessions that matter
ideas.problem: Food tracks under-fuelled days, and session briefs explain the workout, but the two are never connected. An under-fuelled day before a hard ride or a leg day goes unnoticed, and a flat session later gets blamed on fitness.
ideas.proposal: When tomorrow's plan has a hard ride or a lower-body lift, make the 'What to eat next' card on Food say so ('Leg day tomorrow, aim for the full target today'), with a higher carb share. Add one line to the pre-session brief when the previous day was logged as under-fuelled. On Weekly Review, show how sessions felt after fuelled days compared with under-fuelled ones, once enough days are logged.
ideas.benefit: The under-eating habit is caught where it costs the most: right before key sessions.
acceptance_criteria: The day before a planned hard ride or lower-body lift, the Food card names the session and adjusts the suggested split
The pre-session brief mentions an under-fuelled previous day only when food was actually logged that day
Weekly Review shows the fuelled versus under-fuelled comparison only when there are at least 4 logged days on each side
Unlogged days are treated as unknown, never as under-fuelled

ideas.title: One inbox for missing and messy training data
ideas.problem: Gaps in the data are scattered: workouts without feedback, planned sessions that never matched an activity, rides missing heart-rate streams, and benchmarks that went stale. Each one quietly weakens readiness, analysis and plan follow-through, and the athlete only notices by chance.
ideas.proposal: Add a small inbox to Data & Sync, plus a badge in the nav when it isn't empty. List each item with a one-click fix: add feedback, link the session to an activity, re-fetch streams, or mark it as fine. Items the athlete dismisses stay dismissed. Cap the list to the last 30 days so it never turns into a backlog.
ideas.benefit: The data the coaching relies on stays complete, with only a couple of clicks a week.
evidence: docs/roadmap.md open thread: Data-quality inbox (unbuilt half of Sprint 35)
acceptance_criteria: The inbox lists four kinds of items from the last 30 days: missing feedback, unmatched planned sessions, missing HR streams and stale benchmarks
Each item has an inline action that resolves it, and resolved or dismissed items disappear after reload
The nav shows a count badge only when open items exist
Backend tests cover detection for each item kind

ideas.title: An FTP test for when you decide you're ready
ideas.problem: The app keeps the logged 242 W FTP until a new test, but it gives no help with doing one. It has no test workout, no way to pick a good day, and no step that turns the result into the new FTP. Meanwhile every power zone depends on a number that is over half a year old.
ideas.proposal: Add an opt-in 'Plan an FTP test' action on the Athlete page. It is never suggested by the planner on its own. It offers a ramp test and a 20-minute test as .zwo workouts, and picks the next day with good readiness and no hard session the day before. After the ride, the app reads the result (best 20 min × 0.95 or 75% of the last ramp minute) and asks the athlete to confirm it as the new logged FTP.
ideas.benefit: When the athlete chooses to test, it takes one ride and one click to get honest zones again.
acceptance_criteria: Nothing about an FTP test appears in plans or suggestions unless the athlete starts it from the Athlete page
Both test protocols are available as .zwo downloads and as plan entries
After a matching ride, the app shows the computed FTP and requires confirmation before it updates the logged FTP
Tests cover the result calculation for both protocols

ideas.title: Prove the backups actually restore
ideas.problem: Daily and pre-migration backups pass SQLite's integrity check, but no one has restored one and opened the app on it. A backup that passes the integrity check can still fail to migrate or be missing tables, and that would only show up on the day it's needed.
ideas.proposal: Add a restore drill command (and a weekly automatic run). It copies the newest backup to a temporary file, runs the app's migrations against it, runs a few smoke queries (activity count, latest activity date, plan weeks), and records the result. Data & Sync shows 'Last restore drill: OK, 2 days ago', next to the backup status. Document the real restore steps in docs.
ideas.benefit: Confidence that the training history can actually be brought back, checked before it is ever needed.
acceptance_criteria: The drill never touches the live database and deletes its temporary copy
A drill that fails migrations or smoke queries is recorded as failed, with the reason
Data & Sync shows the last drill result and its age
A test runs the drill against a fixture backup

ideas.title: Let stall-block results shape the next suggestions
ideas.problem: Stall blocks are recorded with a snapshot, plan and outcome e1RM, but they only show on Strength. The Dashboard brief never mentions a running block. Later stall suggestions also ignore what worked the last time for the same lift.
ideas.proposal: Show the active block on the Dashboard brief ('Bench stall block, week 2 of 3') and in the pre-session brief for that lift. When a lift stalls again, rank the block types by their past outcome for that lift, or similar lifts, and say why ('Last rep-range block added 4 kg').
ideas.benefit: Stall fixes get smarter over time instead of starting from scratch each time.
evidence: docs/roadmap.md open thread: Stall blocks beyond Strength
acceptance_criteria: The Dashboard brief shows the active block with its week number when one is running
Stall suggestions for a lift with a finished block reference that block's outcome
With no block history, suggestions behave exactly as they do today

ideas.title: See the next four weeks, not just this one
ideas.problem: The Plan page only shows the current week, so training feels like it is planned one week at a time with no direction. The winter arc already knows where the next weeks are heading, but you can only see that in the arc strip, not as upcoming weeks.
ideas.proposal: Under the current week, show a light preview of the next 3–4 weeks, built by code (not the AI) from the winter arc blocks, active goals, mountain trips, illness/re-entry windows and tagged life-load days. Each week is one compact row: block and week number, ride hours, key rides (e.g. 1× sweet spot), lift days, a lighter-week badge, and anything known that bends it (trip, busy week). Only the current week has full day-by-day detail; preview weeks become real plans when they arrive.
ideas.benefit: You can see where training is going and why this week looks the way it does, without the AI having to write detailed plans that would be wrong by the time they arrive.
acceptance_criteria: The Plan page shows the current week in full and the next 3–4 weeks as compact preview rows.
Preview rows come from deterministic code and match the arc's week_target (hours, key rides, lighter weeks).
Known trips, illness or re-entry windows and life-load days appear on the week they affect.
With no winter arc, the preview still shows lift days, goals and known events, or hides cleanly.
The layout stays compact at ~1512px desktop width.

ideas.title: Each new week builds on how the last one went
ideas.problem: The weekly planner gets the block target for this week and next, but not how the previous week went against that target. A key ride that was missed, or a week that ran long, is not carried into the next plan, so each week can feel like it starts from scratch.
ideas.proposal: When a week is generated, add a short 'where you are in the block' note to the planner context: block and week number, last week's arc status (key rides hit or missed, ride hours versus target), follow-through on the previous plan, and whether next week is lighter. Add one carry-over rule: a missed key ride may move into the new week once, unless the new week is lighter or guarded. Show the same one-line note at the top of the generated week.
ideas.benefit: Weeks connect into a real progression, and you can see the reason behind each week in one line.
acceptance_criteria: Planner context includes last week's arc status and follow-through in a compact form.
A generated week shows a one-line block note such as 'Week 3 of 4 in sweet-spot build, last week's SS ride moved here, lighter week next'.
A missed key ride carries over at most once and never into a lighter, sick, re-entry or life-load-guarded day.
Tests cover carry-over, the lighter-week block and a week with no arc.

ideas.title: Gentle strength phases alongside the winter arc
ideas.problem: The winter arc only shapes rides. Lifts progress session by session with occasional stall blocks, so there is no longer rhythm such as a planned lighter week, and heavy leg weeks can line up with the hardest ride weeks.
ideas.proposal: Add an optional, simple strength phase label with dates (e.g. 'Volume', 'Hold', 'Deload week') that can line up with arc blocks. Phases only nudge existing rules: a deload week trims sets on the same lifts, and a hold phase pauses load jumps. They never add new progression rules, never touch the lift 3x anchor goal, and stay off by default.
ideas.benefit: Lifting gets a light longer structure and planned recovery without adding the complexity that felt overwhelming before.
acceptance_criteria: Strength phases are optional and off by default.
A deload week reduces sets without changing exercises or the weekly lift count toward the 3x anchor.
Phases can be suggested to line up with arc lighter weeks, and you confirm them.
Existing progression and stall-block behaviour is unchanged when no phase is active.

ideas.title: Your whole winter on one timeline
ideas.problem: Blocks, mountain trips, goals with target dates, lighter weeks, stall blocks and FTP retests are each shown on their own page. There is no single view of the coming months.
ideas.proposal: Add a horizontal season timeline (e.g. on the Plan or Goals page): arc blocks as coloured bands, lighter weeks marked, trips and events as pins, goal target dates, the active stall block, and a 'you are here' marker. Clicking a week opens its plan or preview. Flat design, compact, read-only first.
ideas.benefit: The big picture is always one glance away, which makes week-to-week training feel purposeful.
acceptance_criteria: One timeline shows arc blocks, lighter weeks, trips, goal dates and the active stall block.
The current week is clearly marked and links to the plan; future weeks link to the preview.
It works with any subset of data present (e.g. no arc).
It fits on a 1512px desktop screen without horizontal page scroll.

ideas.title: A review at the end of every training block
ideas.problem: When an arc block ends, nothing looks back at it. You do not see whether the block delivered, and the next block is not adjusted from what actually happened.
ideas.proposal: When a block ends, create a celebratory block recap: key rides done versus planned, total ride hours, power-curve and aerobic-decoupling change over the block, consistency streak, and one or two plain suggestions for the next block (e.g. 'hours were 20% under, keep the next block at the same hours'). Suggestions are applied only after you confirm.
ideas.benefit: Each block teaches the next one, and you get a motivating moment every few weeks instead of only at season end.
acceptance_criteria: A recap is available for every finished block, with big count-up numbers and visuals rather than tables.
It compares planned and completed key rides and hours for the block.
Next-block suggestions are never applied without confirmation.
Blocks with too little data show an honest 'not enough data' state.

ideas.title: The winter arc adapts when life gets in the way
ideas.problem: The arc has fixed dates. After an illness, a mountain trip or a busy fortnight, the planner either crams missed key rides or the block quietly ends without having done its job.
ideas.proposal: Detect when a block lost 1+ weeks (sick days, re-entry windows, life-load tags, low arc status) and suggest a fix: extend the block by a week and shift later blocks, or accept it and move on. Show the suggestion as a card with a before/after view of the dates. Never cram missed sessions into the remaining weeks.
ideas.benefit: The long-term plan stays realistic instead of falling apart after the first disruption.
acceptance_criteria: A block that lost a week or more shows a suggestion card with extend or accept.
Extending shifts later blocks by the same amount and keeps lighter-week spacing.
Nothing changes until you confirm, and a change can be undone.
Tests cover illness, trip and life-load interruptions.

ideas.title: See where fitness and fatigue are heading
ideas.problem: The app shows past training but cannot say whether the planned weeks ramp load too fast or too slowly, which is exactly the question a longer plan raises.
ideas.proposal: Estimate a fitness/fatigue trend (CTL/ATL-style, using relative effort or power-based load) from history, then project it through the current plan and the 4-week preview. Flag ramps that are too steep or too flat versus the block's purpose. Keep it to one small chart plus a single plain-language line.
ideas.benefit: You can check that the coming weeks build fitness at a safe rate before you ride them.
acceptance_criteria: Past load is computed from logged activities using the FTP valid on each date.
Planned and preview weeks are projected forward with clearly marked estimated values.
A warning shows when the planned weekly ramp exceeds a documented threshold.
Tests cover the load calculation and projection.

ideas.title: One Sunday flow from review to next week's plan
ideas.problem: Wrapping up a week and planning the next takes several pages: weekly review, body check-in, life load, then plan generation. Steps get skipped, so the plan is made with less context.
ideas.proposal: Add a guided Sunday flow: (1) the week's wins and review, (2) a quick body check-in, (3) tag busy days next week, (4) the block note and preview for next week, (5) generate and accept the plan. Each step can be skipped, and the flow remembers where you stopped.
ideas.benefit: Planning becomes a 5-minute ritual, and every plan gets the full context it needs.
acceptance_criteria: One entry point walks through review, check-in, life load, preview and plan generation.
Each step reuses existing components and can be skipped.
Leaving and returning resumes at the same step.
The plan is generated only on your explicit action.

ideas.title: Food targets that follow the training week
ideas.problem: Fuelling advice reacts to single hard sessions, but daily intake targets do not change with block volume. In a big week, eating too little is the main risk.
ideas.proposal: Scale the daily energy and carb guidance on the Food page from the planned week: higher on long or key-ride days and in high-hour blocks, steady in lighter weeks. Show a small 'this week needs more food' hint when planned hours rise compared with recent weeks.
ideas.benefit: Eating keeps up with training, supporting both the under-eating focus and muscle gain.
acceptance_criteria: Daily targets differ for key-ride, long-ride, lift and rest days in the planned week.
A higher-volume week shows a clear eat-more hint.
Targets never drop below the current baseline because of a lighter week.
Tests cover target scaling.

ideas.title: Follow up on aches you mention in session notes
ideas.problem: Session feedback like 'tightness in lower back, probably stress' (Oct 15, pain 2/10) stays a note. Recovery issues and protected body areas only kick in when an issue is opened by hand, and coaching only flags pain at 4/10 or higher.
ideas.proposal: When feedback or a check-in names a body area with pain 1-3, ask the next morning in the check-in: 'Lower back - better, same or worse?'. 'Same' twice opens a light recovery issue (one tap, editable) and offers to protect that area in the lift top-up for a few days. 'Better' closes the thread quietly. Suggest one short mobility routine from the recovery library for that area.
ideas.benefit: Small niggles get caught before they turn into a lost week, without you having to remember to open a recovery issue.
acceptance_criteria: A note naming a body area with pain 1-3 creates a follow-up question in the next morning check-in.
Two 'same' or one 'worse' answer offers a prefilled recovery issue; nothing is created without a tap.
Protecting the area is an explicit choice and expires after a set number of days.
Tests cover area detection from Polish and English notes.

ideas.title: Eat enough on mountain hiking days
ideas.problem: The Oct 19-25 trip is seven hiking days in a row, but food targets follow the planned training week and mountain days are kept out of planning. Long hikes burn far more than a normal day, and under-eating is the known risk.
ideas.proposal: On days tagged Mountains, raise the Food target from the hike estimate (planned hours and elevation if a saved route exists, else a typical TPN day). Show a short trip fuelling card before the trip: daily kcal and carbs, snacks per hour on the trail, and a packing list of easy foods from your saved products. After each day, fill in the burn from the synced hike.
ideas.benefit: You come back from the trip without a week-long energy hole, which also protects muscle gain and the re-entry week.
evidence: backend/app/services/hike_detail.py and route_planner.py: duration and elevation
acceptance_criteria: Mountains-tagged days get a higher target than rest days, sized from route or default hike estimate.
Mountain days stay out of the training plan and load model.
A pre-trip card lists daily targets and trail snack amounts.
Targets update from the synced hike after each day.

ideas.title: Celebrate the 300-day streak and other milestones
ideas.problem: The daily streak is at 286 days and will pass 300 on Oct 29, just after the mountain trip. Today it is a single number on the Dashboard; big moments go by unnoticed.
ideas.proposal: Detect milestones (streak 100/200/300/365 days, lift-3x weeks in a row, year km thresholds, first sweet-spot ride in a month) and show a one-time full-screen celebration with a count-up number, a day grid of the streak and a few highlights from that stretch. Keep a small milestone shelf on Records.
ideas.benefit: Long consistency gets the moment it deserves, which is a strong motivation driver for you.
acceptance_criteria: Each milestone celebrates once and can be reopened from Records.
Celebration uses big animated numbers and visuals, not tables.
Light recovery days keep counting toward the streak as they do now.
Tests cover milestone detection.

ideas.title: Mark unlogged food days with one tap
ideas.problem: Only 6 of the recent days have food logged. Unlogged days are treated as unknown, so the under-eating trend rests on a few days and misses busy days, which are the most likely to be short.
ideas.proposal: On the next morning, if yesterday has no or very little food logged, ask one question on the Food page and check-in: 'Yesterday was: ate less than usual / about normal / ate more / skip'. Store a rough estimate flagged as a guess, keep it out of logged totals, and use it only in the weekly under-eating read.
ideas.benefit: The weekly food picture gets honest without making logging tedious.
evidence: get_recent_context nutrition: logged_days 6, avg gap -434 kcal
acceptance_criteria: A day with no log gets one prompt at most, and 'skip' is respected.
Rough days are visibly marked as guesses and never mixed into logged totals.
The weekly under-eating summary counts them separately.
Tests cover the prompt rule.

ideas.title: Protect sleep when stress and sleep debt stack up
ideas.problem: Readiness is red today: sleep debt 6.1 h over 7 nights, stress 4/5, resting HR +3. The app tells you to swap today's session, but nothing helps you pay the debt back or keeps late sessions from making it worse.
ideas.proposal: When sleep debt is 'risk' and stress is high for 2+ days, show a short payback plan: target bedtime for the next 3 nights from your median sleep, prefer morning or early-evening slots for remaining sessions, and keep sessions under 60 min until debt is back to 'ok'. Show how the debt falls each day.
ideas.benefit: Recovery comes from the cause instead of only skipping sessions, so the lift-3x anchor and key rides survive busy weeks.
acceptance_criteria: The plan appears only when sleep debt is at risk and stress is high on 2+ days.
It never removes lift sessions, only shortens or moves them.
Progress shows the debt shrinking night by night.
Tests cover the trigger.

ideas.title: Estimate power for outdoor rides without a power meter
ideas.problem: Outdoor rides have no power meter, so ride balance falls back to HR zones and load mixes power-based and HR-based numbers. Winter outdoor rides will look easier or harder than they were.
ideas.proposal: Estimate average and normalized power for outdoor rides from speed, elevation, weight, bike type and a simple drag model, using the detailed streams already stored. Mark the values as estimated, use them for load and ride type only, never for records or FTP.
ideas.benefit: Indoor and outdoor rides count on the same scale, so the winter arc and fitness forecast stay honest.
evidence: backend/app/services/ride_balance.py: HR fallback for outdoor rides
acceptance_criteria: Outdoor rides without power get an estimate flagged as estimated.
Estimates never enter personal records, power curve or FTP.
Calibration check on rides that have both is within a stated error band.
Tests cover the physics model.

ideas.title: Pick indoor or outdoor for each ride from the forecast
ideas.problem: Winter weather decides whether a planned ride goes outside or onto Zwift, but the plan does not say which, and weather is only shown as current conditions.
ideas.proposal: For each planned ride in the next 7 days, use the existing 16-day forecast to tag it 'good for outside' or 'Zwift day' (temperature, rain, wind, daylight). Key rides default to Zwift so the structure holds; long easy rides prefer the best-weather day.
ideas.benefit: Less daily deciding, and outdoor rides land on the days that suit them.
acceptance_criteria: Planned rides show an indoor or outdoor tag with the reason.
Key interval rides stay indoor by default.
Missing forecast falls back silently.
Tests cover the rule.

ideas.title: Ask the coach about any card or chart
ideas.problem: The in-app coach chat is best when it knows what you are looking at, but it is opened from the drawer, so questions about a chart ('why is relative effort below range?') need retyping the context.
ideas.proposal: Add a small 'Ask coach' action on key cards (relative effort, readiness, ride balance, muscle-gain check, food week, fitness forecast). It opens a chat thread linked to that card with the card's data attached, and the thread shows up again next to the card.
ideas.benefit: The coach chat becomes part of reading the dashboard, without switching apps.
evidence: Dashboard relative effort, readiness, Metrics ride balance
acceptance_criteria: At least five cards offer 'Ask coach' with their data attached.
Threads are linked to the card and can be reopened from it.
Existing drawer chat keeps working.
Tests cover the context payload.
